title: What is the difference between RDS Multi-AZ (synchronous standby for high availability/failover) and read replicas (asynchronous, for read scaling)?

s1_definition.profdef: RDS Multi-AZ provisions a synchronous standby replica of the primary database in a different Availability Zone; every committed write is replicated to the standby before being acknowledged, and if the primary fails, RDS automatically fails over to the standby, so Multi-AZ is purely about high availability and durability, not performance. A read replica is an asynchronous copy that you can send read-only queries to, used to scale read throughput by offloading reads from the primary; because replication is asynchronous there is some replication lag, and a replica does not provide automatic failover unless you explicitly promote it. In short, Multi-AZ is for availability through synchronous standby and automatic failover, while read replicas are for read scaling through asynchronous copies.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the main ledger at National Bank of India. Multi-AZ is like having a second clerk in another branch who writes down every single transaction at the exact same moment as the main clerk, so if the main clerk suddenly leaves, the second clerk instantly becomes the main clerk with an identical, up-to-the-second ledger — but customers never go to that second clerk for answers; they wait silently as a backup. A read replica is different: it is like photocopying the ledger every few seconds and placing the copies in several reading rooms, so that many people who only want to read the ledger can do so without crowding the main clerk, accepting that a copy might be a few seconds behind.
s1_definition.oneliner: Multi-AZ is a hidden synchronous twin for automatic failover and availability, while read replicas are asynchronous copies you read from to scale read traffic.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** RDS Multi-AZ provisions a synchronous standby replica of the primary database in a different Availability Zone; every committed write is replicated to the standby before being acknowledged, and if the primary fails, RDS automatically fails over to the standby, so Multi-AZ is purely about high availability and durability, not performance. A read replica is an asynchronous copy that you can send read-only queries to, used to scale read throughput by offloading reads from the primary; because replication is asynchronous there is some replication lag, and a replica does not provide automatic failover unless you explicitly promote it. In short, Multi-AZ is for availability through synchronous standby and automatic failover, while read replicas are for read scaling through asynchronous copies.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the main ledger at National Bank of India. Multi-AZ is like having a second clerk in another branch who writes down every single transaction at the exact same moment as the main clerk, so if the main clerk suddenly leaves, the second clerk instantly becomes the main clerk with an identical, up-to-the-second ledger — but customers never go to that second clerk for answers; they wait silently as a backup. A read replica is different: it is like photocopying the ledger every few seconds and placing the copies in several reading rooms, so that many people who only want to read the ledger can do so without crowding the main clerk, accepting that a copy might be a few seconds behind.

**One line to remember:** Multi-AZ is a hidden synchronous twin for automatic failover and availability, while read replicas are asynchronous copies you read from to scale read traffic.

sections.s2_technical:
Multi-AZ is about staying up. When you enable it, RDS creates a standby in another Availability Zone and replicates synchronously, meaning a write is not acknowledged to the application until both the primary and the standby have it. This keeps the standby perfectly current. The standby is not readable — you cannot send queries to it — it exists purely to take over. On failure of the primary, RDS flips the single endpoint's DNS to the standby and promotes it, usually in one to two minutes, and the application reconnects to the same endpoint automatically.

```java
// With Multi-AZ, the app uses ONE endpoint for reads and writes.
String writerEndpoint = "jdbc:postgresql://nbi-ledger.rds.amazonaws.com:5432/ledger";
// You never connect to the standby directly; it is invisible until failover.
```

Read replicas are about handling more reads. A read replica is a separate, readable database instance that receives changes asynchronously from the primary. Because it is asynchronous, the replica can be slightly behind the primary, which is called replication lag. You direct read-only traffic — reports, analytics, dashboards — to the replica's own endpoint, freeing the primary to handle writes and latency-sensitive reads.

```java
// With read replicas, the app sends writes and reads to DIFFERENT endpoints.
String writerEndpoint = "jdbc:postgresql://nbi-ledger.rds.amazonaws.com:5432/ledger";      // writes
String readerEndpoint = "jdbc:postgresql://nbi-ledger-ro.rds.amazonaws.com:5432/ledger";   // heavy reads
```

The failover behavior is the key contrast. Multi-AZ failover is automatic and the endpoint stays the same. A read replica does not fail over automatically; it can be manually promoted to a standalone primary, which breaks its replication link and is a deliberate recovery action, not an automatic safety net.

These two features are complementary, not alternatives. A production banking database typically has both: Multi-AZ for availability and one or more read replicas for read scaling. A senior nuance: because read replicas are asynchronous, you must never read something from a replica that you require to be perfectly up to date, such as a balance you just updated, because the replica may not have that write yet — read-after-write consistency must come from the primary. Aurora blurs this line by offering replicas that are both readable and fast-failover targets, and cross-Region read replicas additionally serve disaster recovery and low-latency local reads.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's ledger must survive the loss of an entire Availability Zone without data loss and without a human intervening. This is exactly what Multi-AZ solves: the synchronous standby is always current and RDS fails over to it automatically.

Problem 2 — During the day, dashboards and reports fire thousands of read queries that compete with live transfers and slow them down. This is exactly what read replicas solve: those reads go to an asynchronous copy, keeping the primary free for writes.

Problem 3 — A developer wrongly tries to confirm a just-completed transfer by reading from a replica and sees a stale balance because the replica lagged. This shows exactly why read-after-write must use the primary.

We will write a small routing simulator. `DatabaseCluster` has a primary with a synchronous standby and a set of asynchronous read replicas with a lag. `QueryRouter` sends writes and consistency-critical reads to the primary, routes bulk reads to a replica, and performs an automatic failover to the standby. The demo shows a write, a report on a replica, a failover, and the stale-read pitfall.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a ledger cluster with Multi-AZ on and one read replica lagging two seconds. We perform a write, a bulk report read, a consistency-critical read, a mistaken replica read, and a failover.

Step 1. A transfer write is sent. The router sends it to the primary, and because Multi-AZ is on, the synchronous standby in another Availability Zone receives the same write before the commit is acknowledged. Both copies now hold the write identically.

Step 2. A month-end report, a heavy read, is routed to the read replica. The replica is an asynchronous copy about two seconds behind, which is perfectly fine for an aggregate report. The primary is not touched, so live transfers keep full speed.

Step 3. A balance read that must reflect the just-completed write is routed to the primary. Because the primary always has the latest committed data, the read-after-write result is correct.

Step 4. To illustrate the pitfall, the same balance is read from the replica. Because the replica lags two seconds, it might not yet have the write, so it could return a stale balance. This is why consistency-critical reads must never go to a replica.

Step 5. The primary's Availability Zone fails. Because Multi-AZ is on, RDS automatically promotes the synchronous standby, keeping the same endpoint and losing no committed data. Had there been only a read replica and no Multi-AZ, recovery would have required a manual promotion.

Step 6. The final output logs the write, the report on the replica, the correct consistent read, the stale-read warning, and the automatic failover.

```
2026-10-29 02:20:00 [INFO] WRITE transfer: primary applied 'debit SAV2001 50000' + synchronous standby in sync
2026-10-29 02:20:00 [INFO] REPORT (bulk read): replica-1 served 'sum of all transfers today' (lag 2s, acceptable for reports)
2026-10-29 02:20:00 [INFO] BALANCE right after write: primary served 'balance SAV2001' (read-after-write correct)
2026-10-29 02:20:00 [WARNING] If balance read from replica: replica served 'balance SAV2001' but may be 2s stale — WRONG for read-after-write
2026-10-29 02:20:00 [SEVERE] Primary AZ failed!
2026-10-29 02:20:00 [INFO] Failover: synchronous standby promoted automatically, zero data loss (automatic, same endpoint)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
RDS Multi-AZ and read replicas solve two completely different problems, and I am careful never to confuse them. Multi-AZ is about availability. When I enable it, RDS keeps a synchronous standby in a second Availability Zone, and every committed write goes to both the primary and the standby before it is acknowledged, so the standby is always perfectly current. That standby is not readable — it exists only to take over. If the primary fails, RDS automatically fails over to the standby in a minute or two behind the same endpoint, so my application just reconnects with no data loss and no manual action.

Read replicas are about performance, specifically scaling reads. A read replica is a separate, readable instance that receives changes asynchronously from the primary, so it can be slightly behind, which we call replication lag. I point heavy read-only traffic like reports and dashboards at the replica's own endpoint so the primary is left free for writes and latency-sensitive reads. A read replica does not fail over automatically; promoting it is a deliberate manual recovery action that breaks its replication link.

The contrast that matters most is the failover behavior and the consistency guarantee. Multi-AZ failover is automatic and transparent on the same endpoint, while a replica must be manually promoted. And because replicas are asynchronous, I must never serve a read-after-write that has to be perfectly current from a replica — if I just updated a balance and need to confirm it, I read that from the primary, because the replica may not have the write yet.

At National Bank of India I ran the ledger with both features together, which is the normal production pattern. Multi-AZ gave me automatic failover so an Availability Zone outage promoted the synchronous standby in about ninety seconds with zero data loss, and two read replicas absorbed the month-end reporting load so live transfers stayed fast. I explicitly routed consistency-critical reads, like confirming a balance right after a transfer, to the primary, because once a developer read a just-updated balance from a lagging replica and saw a stale value — that incident is exactly why I treat Multi-AZ as availability and read replicas as read scaling, never as interchangeable.
